subChunks.title: Pipeline Stages, Test Gates & Deployment Strategies
subChunks.hookHtml: Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) is the practice that transforms code commits into reliable production deployments. A well-designed pipeline is a safety net — it catches bugs before users see them, enforces quality gates automatically, and enables deployment frequency that would be impossible with manual processes.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Continuous Integration (CI)

Every code change triggers an automated pipeline that verifies the change integrates correctly with the codebase. The key discipline: commit to main frequently (at least daily) so integration problems are caught small. Long-lived feature branches accumulate divergence — the longer they live, the more painful the merge.

A typical CI pipeline:

  1. Checkout: pull the source code
  2. Build: compile — fails fast on syntax errors
  3. Unit tests: fast, isolated — milliseconds each
  4. Integration tests: slower — may spin up a test DB or use Testcontainers
  5. Code analysis: linting, style checks, SAST (static security analysis)
  6. Package: build the artifact (JAR, Docker image)
  7. Publish: push artifact to registry

Continuous Deployment (CD)

Automatically deploy every build that passes CI to production (or to staging/prod via promotion gates). Requires: feature flags (to decouple deploy from release), comprehensive automated tests, observability, and fast rollback capability.

Deployment Strategies

Rolling deployment: gradually replace instances with the new version — e.g. update 25% of instances, wait for health checks, continue. Zero-downtime. Old and new versions run simultaneously briefly — requires backward-compatible API and DB changes.

Blue/Green deployment: maintain two identical environments. Traffic goes to Blue (v1). Deploy v2 to Green. Flip load balancer from Blue to Green. Instant switchover with instant rollback (flip back to Blue). Expensive: requires double infrastructure.

Canary deployment: route a small percentage of traffic (e.g. 1%) to the new version. Monitor metrics. Gradually increase if healthy. Abort if error rate rises. Best risk management — real users, real data, tiny blast radius.

Quality Gates

Hard stops in the pipeline that block deployment if criteria are not met:

  • Test coverage must be ≥ X% (measured by JaCoCo)
  • No new critical/high security vulnerabilities (SAST scan)
  • Performance test p99 within threshold
  • All tests must pass (zero failures)

Feature Flags

Decouple deploy from release. Deploy the code but keep the feature inactive (flag off). Enable for internal users first, then % of users, then all. Enables safe incremental rollout and instant kill-switch without re-deployment.

storyBeats.text: Before CI/CD the Academy deployed on Friday afternoons. Engineers manually built artifacts, copied files to servers, ran smoke tests by hand. Deployments took four hours. They happened monthly. Bugs found on Monday had been lurking for a month of commits. After CI/CD, deployments happened ten times a day, automatically, in twelve minutes. Bugs were caught in the pipeline before anyone noticed.

storyBeats.speaker: Release Lead Coren
storyBeats.text: Continuous integration is a practice, not a tool. The tool is GitHub Actions or Jenkins. The practice is: every developer commits to main (or short-lived branches) daily, and every commit triggers a pipeline that tells you within minutes whether the change is safe. If the pipeline is red, fixing it is the team's top priority.

storyBeats.speaker: Release Lead Coren
storyBeats.text: Canary deployment is the most sophisticated and the safest. You deploy to 1% of traffic first. If your new spell-casting algorithm has a bug, only 1% of users encounter it — and your monitoring catches the error rate spike before you roll to 100%. The blast radius is controlled. You can abort and roll back in seconds.

storyBeats.speaker: Pipeline as code — GitHub Actions
storyBeats.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '21' }
      - run: mvn verify        # build + all tests
      - run: mvn jacoco:report  # coverage
      - name: Quality gate
        run: |
          coverage=$(cat target/site/jacoco/index.html | ...)
          if [ $coverage -lt 80 ]; then exit 1; fi

storyBeats.speaker: Release Lead Coren
storyBeats.text: Feature flags are not optional in a canary strategy — they are the mechanism. You deploy the code for a new feature but the flag is off. You test in production with real infrastructure and real data, with flag on for your team only. When confidence is high, you ramp the flag to 10%, 50%, 100%. No re-deployment required. And the kill-switch is instant.

learningObjectives: Describe the stages of a CI pipeline in order and explain what each stage verifies
Distinguish rolling, blue/green, and canary deployment strategies and identify the trade-off of each
Explain what a quality gate is and give three examples of criteria a gate might enforce
Describe how feature flags decouple deployment from release
commonMistakes: Long-lived feature branches — diverge from main, causing painful merges and delayed integration feedback
Using blue/green deployment without considering DB schema compatibility — both versions must work with the same schema during transition
Setting quality gates too low initially and never raising them — the gate becomes meaningless
Deploying feature flags as code toggles that require redeployment — defeats the purpose; use a runtime flag service
assessmentCriteria: Can draw and label a CI pipeline with at least 5 stages in correct order
Can explain the key difference between blue/green and canary deployment and why canary is lower risk
Can describe what needs to be true for a rolling deployment to be safe (backward-compatible changes)
Can explain what 'decouple deploy from release' means and why it reduces deployment risk
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain CI/CD to a team that currently deploys manually once a month. What is the value of deploying more frequently? What is the risk and how do deployment strategies (canary, blue/green) manage it?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following design questions:

  1. Your team currently has: a 20-minute build, 45-minute integration test suite, and 5-minute deployment. Total pipeline: 70 minutes. How would you restructure the pipeline to get faster feedback without removing tests?
  2. You are deploying a new version that changes a database column from VARCHAR(50) to VARCHAR(200). Which deployment strategy can you use safely, and what must be true about the migration order (code vs DB change)?
  3. You notice the error rate rises to 3% immediately after a canary deployment reaches 10% of traffic. What do you do?
  4. Describe a feature flag implementation that would let you enable a new spell-ranking algorithm for 10% of users without re-deployment.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Restructure for fast feedback:
   - Keep unit tests (fast, seconds) in the main CI pipeline — run immediately on every push
   - Parallelise integration tests: split into 4 parallel jobs (45min → ~12min)
   - Move performance/regression tests to a nightly pipeline — not every commit
   - Result: fast feedback (build + unit tests) in ~5min, full integration validation in ~20min, performance weekly

2. VARCHAR(50) → VARCHAR(200) is backward-compatible (expanding, not contracting). Safe with rolling deployment.
   Order: DB migration FIRST (widen column), then deploy new application code.
   Old code continues to work with the wider column. New code benefits from the wider column.
   Never do it in reverse — deploying code that writes VARCHAR(200) to a VARCHAR(50) column causes truncation/errors.

3. Canary error spike response:
   - Immediately halt the canary rollout — freeze at 10%
   - Route all traffic back to v1 (0% canary)
   - Investigate the error type from logs/traces — find root cause
   - Fix the code, redeploy, restart the canary at 1%
   Do NOT roll forward hoping it resolves — error rates don't self-heal.

4. Feature flag for spell ranking:
   - In the database or a config service, store a flag: {"spellRankingV2": {"enabled": true, "rolloutPercent": 10}}
   - At runtime: hash(userId) % 100 < rolloutPercent → use v2 algorithm; else → use v1
   - To change: update the config value in the service. No code change, no deployment.
   - To kill: set rolloutPercent to 0. Instant, no deployment needed.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design a CI/CD pipeline for the Academy's spell service. The service has: 200 unit tests (fast), 50 integration tests (each needs a DB), and a canary deployment to 3 production regions. Answer:

  1. Draw the full pipeline stages from commit to 100% production rollout
  2. Which tests run in which stages and why?
  3. What quality gates do you enforce and at which stage?
  4. How do you handle a DB schema migration that must happen before code deployment?
  5. What metrics do you monitor during canary and at what threshold do you abort?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Pipeline stages:
   Commit → Build (2min) → Unit Tests (30s) → [Quality Gate: 80% coverage, 0 failures]
   → Integration Tests in parallel (15min with Testcontainers) → [Gate: 0 failures]
   → SAST Security Scan (3min) → [Gate: no new CRITICAL vulns]
   → Package Docker Image → Push to Registry
   → Deploy to Staging (canary 100%) → Smoke Tests
   → Deploy to Prod Region 1 (canary 5%) → Monitor 10min
   → Ramp to 25% → Monitor 10min → 100% → Done

2. Unit tests: stage 2 — fast, run on every commit. Isolation: no DB, pure Java.
   Integration tests: stage 4 — need real DB (Testcontainers spins up Postgres). Slower, run on main/PR.

3. Quality gates:
   After unit tests: 80% line coverage (JaCoCo), zero test failures
   After integration tests: zero failures, all endpoints return expected responses
   After SAST: no new CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerabilities

4. DB migration order:
   Run Flyway migration before deploying new application code.
   The migration must be backward-compatible with the currently running code version (add-only, no renames/deletes).
   CI pipeline: migration step runs in staging and prod BEFORE the code deployment step.

5. Canary monitoring:
   Metrics: error rate, p99 latency, JVM heap usage, GC pause time
   Abort threshold: error rate > 1% (baseline 0.1%), or p99 latency > 2× baseline for 5 minutes
   Monitoring window: 10 minutes at each traffic percentage before ramping
   Automatic rollback: if Prometheus alert fires during canary window, trigger rollback to previous version

questions.prompt: In a CI pipeline, which stage runs first to provide the fastest feedback on a broken build?
questions.explanation: Compilation fails in seconds for syntax errors and missing dependencies — the fastest possible feedback. Running tests on code that doesn't compile is wasteful. The pipeline stages are ordered fastest-to-slowest: compile → unit tests (seconds) → integration tests (minutes) → security scan → deployment. Fail early and fail fast.

questions.prompt: A canary deployment routes 5% of traffic to v2. The v2 error rate is 8% while v1 is 0.2%. What should happen next?
options: Continue the rollout — 5% is a small sample and may not be representative
Increase to 50% traffic to get a better sample size
Abort the rollout, roll back to 0% canary, investigate the errors
Disable the circuit breaker to allow more requests through
questions.answer: Abort the rollout, roll back to 0% canary, investigate the errors
questions.explanation: An 8% error rate on v2 (vs 0.2% baseline on v1) is a clear signal of a regression. Continuing or expanding the canary would expose more users to failures. Immediately route all traffic back to v1, investigate the root cause from logs and traces, fix the bug, and restart the canary process from scratch after fixing.

questions.prompt: You want to test a new spell recommendation algorithm on real production traffic for 2% of users without deploying new code when you change the percentage. What is the correct approach?
options: Deploy two separate services and route 2% of traffic at the load balancer level
Use a feature flag service where the rollout percentage is a configuration value changed at runtime
Deploy in blue/green and route 2% to the green environment
questions.answer: Use a feature flag service where the rollout percentage is a configuration value changed at runtime
questions.explanation: Feature flags allow changing the percentage without redeployment — the whole point is decoupling deploy from release. Hardcoding requires a code change and redeploy to change the percentage. Two separate services and blue/green also require operational changes to adjust the split. A feature flag service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or a simple DB-backed config) lets you change from 2% to 50% to 0% with no code changes and instant effect.
